title: SYSK Selects: Is brain size related to intelligence?
summary: SYSK Selects rerun (originally July 2014) in which Josh and Chuck explore whether brain size relates to intelligence. Chuck introduces the episode as his pick from the archives. They cover genetics of brain size (twin studies, beta-catenin gene experiments in mice, MCPH-associated and EMX2 genes), brain size relative to body size (encephalization quotient), autism and rapid early brain growth, ADHD and brain volume, sleep clearing brain waste, measurement problems with brain size and IQ tests, Einstein's brain, the Michael McDaniel sex-differences study, the Harvard "tether hypothesis" about early human brain expansion, neural chemistry versus neuron count, dolphin and animal intelligence, a city mice versus country mice brain study, a pornography and brain volume study, and listener mail about a listener's wife with breast cancer during pregnancy.

segments.title: Selects intro
segments.summary: Chuck introduces this Saturday Selects episode, picking the July 2014 episode on whether brain size relates to intelligence. The episode opens with the hosts' banter.

segments.title: Brain size and intelligence overview
segments.summary: The hosts introduce the question: larger brain size correlates with intelligence only up to a point. Sperm whale brains are larger than human brains, so the ratio of brain to body size is considered next. There is no definitive answer.

segments.title: Genetics and brain size
segments.summary: Twin studies suggest genetics plays a role in brain size, since identical twins are more similar in brain size than fraternal twins. Researchers have identified genes linked to brain growth, including beta-catenin, which enlarged brains and improved cognition in injected mice, though many mice died.

segments.title: Microcephaly gene and EMX2
segments.summary: The hosts discuss a gene associated with microcephaly, linked to small heads and brains and cognitive impairment. They then discuss EMX2, which affects growth of cortical subdivisions tied to sensory input and motor output; too little or too much expression hurts behavioral performance, using baseball hitting as an example.

segments.title: Early brain growth, autism, ADHD and sleep
segments.summary: Disproportionate brain growth in the first year has been linked to autism. Environment is also considered important. Adolescents with ADHD may have brains three to four percent smaller, and brains shrink with age without necessarily losing function. Newly found brain clearance during sleep is mentioned.

segments.title: Measuring brain size and intelligence
segments.summary: The hosts discuss how brain size is measured in different ways, including body-proportion measures like encephalization quotient, and how intelligence itself is hard to measure. Encephalization quotient works well comparing mammal species but less so beyond mammals. Human brains weigh around three pounds and use a large share of energy.

segments.title: Einstein's brain and sex differences
segments.summary: Einstein's brain was of ordinary size but some regions were larger. Men tend to have a slightly larger brain mass than women, which the hosts argue does not mean men are more intelligent. They discuss psychologist Michael McDaniel's 2005 study claiming men score higher, criticizing its use of SAT scores converted to IQ.

segments.title: Tether hypothesis and neural connectivity
segments.summary: A December 2017 New York Times report covered a Harvard neuroscientists' tether hypothesis: early primate neurons were tightly tethered, and as brains grew those tethers loosened, allowing new circuits and intelligence. A competing view holds that neural chemistry and neurotransmitter complexity matter more than neuron count.

segments.title: Animal intelligence
segments.summary: The hosts argue that comparing intelligence across species such as dolphins and humans is largely futile because their experiences of the world differ radically.

segments.title: City mice, country mice and pornography studies
segments.summary: A study in Proceedings of the Royal Society B reported that city mice and voles had larger brains than country ones, but only two of ten species showed this, and the hosts criticize the headline-driven reporting. They also discuss a German study linking pornography use to smaller striatum volume, noting self-reported data and that causation is unclear.

segments.title: Listener mail: help for a fan in need
segments.summary: A listener writes that his wife, pregnant with their first child, was diagnosed with stage four breast cancer and is undergoing chemo. The hosts read his requests to promote his tumblr, a 150-mile charity bike ride, and a shout-out to his wife, nicknamed the Mayor.

segments.title: Sign-off
segments.summary: The hosts give contact info for Twitter, Facebook, email, and the website, and sign off.
